260.title: For heaven's sake (Avot 2:12)
260.hook: let your friend's property be as dear as your own, and do everything for heaven's sake
260.howItsDone: Many Jews use the phrase leshem shamayim for acts done with a higher purpose, and some say a short declaration of intention before performing a commandment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Joshua's warning about the begrudging eye. Your line was a good eye. Did you say congratulations and mean it? Today, the pious one of the five students. Day two hundred sixty.

Oh, for heaven's sake. You've probably said it this week. When the printer jammed, when the dog got into the trash, when someone took the last parking spot. It's what people say when they're fed up. But that phrase has a much older life. In Hebrew, leshem shamayim, for the sake of heaven, isn't a sigh of frustration at all. It's a way of living. And it comes from Rabbi Yose, the student his teacher called the pious one.
screen: `OH, FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE.` → `A SIGH, OR A WAY OF LIVING?` → `RABBI YOSE, THE PIOUS ONE.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Yose says three things. First: let your friend's property be as dear to you as your own. Treat the borrowed ladder like it's yours. Better, actually, because it isn't. Return it on time, clean, working. Second: prepare yourself to learn Torah, because it isn't an inheritance. You can inherit a house from your parents. You can't inherit their learning. Even the child of the greatest scholar starts from the first page and does the work himself. And third: let all your deeds be for the sake of heaven. Heaven, here, is a respectful way of saying God. So the line means: whatever you do, let it point toward something higher than yourself. Not only praying and studying. Everything. Later Jewish teachers took this very far. Maimonides wrote that even eating and sleeping can be for the sake of heaven, if you do them to keep your body healthy so you can do good. The meal is still a meal. The nap is still a nap. What changes is the reason. See how the three parts fit. Other people's things matter as much as yours. What's worth having has to be earned, not handed down. And ordinary life can be aimed at something holy. The printer jam and the parking lot are still part of it. Even the moment you want to say oh, for heaven's sake can be a moment to remember what the phrase really means.
screen: `YOUR FRIEND'S THINGS AS YOUR OWN.` · `LEARNING ISN'T AN INHERITANCE.` · `ALL YOUR DEEDS FOR HEAVEN.` · `EVEN EATING AND SLEEPING.` · then, large: `FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: aim one ordinary thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you'll do today that feels completely ordinary. Making lunch. Commuting. Answering email. Returning something you borrowed. Now ask: what higher purpose could this serve? Feeding someone well. Getting somewhere to help. Keeping a promise. You don't have to change the act. Just let the reason point a little higher. The bell holds the time.
For heaven's sake. Leshem shamayim: Rabbi Yose's teaching that all your deeds, even the ordinary ones, can be done for the sake of heaven.
Your line: for heaven's sake. Today, return one thing you borrowed, in good shape, and let one ordinary task point higher. Day two hundred sixty.

261.title: Not a routine (Avot 2:13)
261.hook: don't make your prayer a fixed routine but a plea for mercy
261.howItsDone: Jewish prayer follows fixed texts in the siddur, said three times a day, and many Jews work at kavanah, inner intention, and add personal requests in their own words within the Amidah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Yose: let all your deeds be for the sake of heaven. Your line was for heaven's sake. Did you return what you borrowed? Day two hundred sixty-one.

Love you, bye. You've said it at the end of a phone call so fast that it came out as one word. Loveyoubye. You meant it, sort of. But your mind was already on the next thing. Anything we say every day can wear smooth like that, like a stone in a river. Jewish prayer is said every day, three times a day, mostly from a fixed prayer book. So the rabbis faced a real problem. How do you say the same words thousands of times without them turning into loveyoubye? Rabbi Shimon, the fourth of the five students, has an answer.
screen: `LOVEYOUBYE.` → `A STONE WORN SMOOTH.` → `THE SAME WORDS, THREE TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Shimon says: be careful with the Shema and with prayer. And when you pray, don't make your prayer keva, fixed, but a plea for mercy before God. Then he gives a verse from the prophet Joel. That chapter contains a famous line, which in the old King James wording reads, "rend your heart, and not your garments." Tear open your heart, not just your clothes. The outward sign isn't enough. The Talmud stops to ask what keva, fixed, actually means here, and gives several answers. One sage says: prayer that feels like a burden, a chore to get through. Others say: prayer that isn't said as a real request, the way a person actually pleads. And another says: prayer where you can't add anything new. One rabbi admitted that he could add something new, but was afraid he'd lose his place in the prayers. It's a very human moment. Here's the interesting part. Nobody in this conversation says throw out the prayer book. The fixed words stay. They hold a whole community together, in every city, in the same language, at the same times. What Rabbi Shimon asks is that you not let the fixed words make you fixed. Fill them with something, each time. The Hebrew word for that inner attention is kavanah: intention, direction, aiming the heart. The words are the same. You're the one who arrives new. Rabbi Shimon ends with one more line: don't be wicked in your own eyes. Don't give up on yourself. The plea for mercy starts with believing it's worth asking.
screen: `KEVA: FIXED, ROUTINE.` · `REND YOUR HEART, NOT YOUR GARMENTS.` · `WHAT DOES FIXED MEAN?` · `KAVANAH: AIMING THE HEART.` · then, large: `NOT ROTE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one thing freshly. Settle, and breathe. Think of words you say every day on autopilot. A blessing, a greeting, a goodnight, love you, bye. Pick one. Now say it silently, very slowly, and mean every word, as if you'd never said it before. If you pray, you can add one sentence of your own to a prayer you already know, in your own words. If you don't, just let one honest sentence of what you need rise up. The bell holds the time.
Not a routine. Rabbi Shimon's warning: don't make your prayer keva, fixed, but a real plea from the heart, with kavanah.
Your line: not rote. Today, catch one thing you say on autopilot, and say it again slowly, meaning it. Day two hundred sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 261 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KNOW WHO YOU WORK FOR.`

262.title: Know who you work for (Avot 2:14)
262.hook: be eager to learn, and know before whom you labor
262.howItsDone: Jewish learning encourages hard questions, and many synagogues display the words 'know before whom you stand' above the ark as a reminder during prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Shimon asked that prayer never become a routine. Your line was not rote. What did you say slowly and mean? Today, the last of the five students. Day two hundred sixty-two.

There's a question every kid eventually asks at the dinner table, usually when a guest is there. How do you know God is real? Or, why do we even do this? And the adults glance at each other, and somebody says, eat your peas. Most of us have been on one side of that table or the other. Today's sage is Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, the student whose answer won, the one with the good heart. And his saying starts by telling you to be ready for that question.
screen: `THE QUESTION AT THE DINNER TABLE.` → `EAT YOUR PEAS.` → `ELAZAR BEN ARACH.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Elazar says: be eager to learn Torah. Know what to answer an apikoros. And know before whom you toil, and that your employer can be trusted to pay you the wage of your work. Take the strange word first. Apikoros comes from the name Epicurus, a Greek philosopher who taught that the gods, if they exist, don't care about human beings. In rabbinic Hebrew, an apikoros came to mean a scoffer, someone who mocks the faith and its teachers. Rabbi Elazar doesn't say avoid them, or shout them down. He says study well enough to answer. Don't be caught with only eat your peas. And some later teachers add a quiet point: the hardest skeptic is often the voice inside your own head, at two in the morning. Knowing what to answer means learning enough to face your own questions honestly. Then the second half. Know before whom you toil. All your learning and your work happen in front of someone. There's a related line in the Talmud that many synagogues display above the ark: know before whom you stand. And then, a picture from the workplace. Your employer is trustworthy, and will pay your wages. The employer, in this saying, is God. The work you put into learning and living well isn't lost, even when no one else seems to notice. Put together: learn hard, be ready for hard questions, and remember who you're really working for.
screen: `BE EAGER TO LEARN.` · `APIKOROS: FROM EPICURUS.` · `KNOW BEFORE WHOM YOU TOIL.` · `YOUR EMPLOYER WILL PAY.` · then, large: `KNOW WHO YOU WORK FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet one hard question. Settle, and breathe. Let one hard question come up, about faith, or meaning, or why people do what they do. Your own, or one a child or friend has asked you. Don't rush to answer it. Just hold it honestly. Then ask: what's one thing I could learn this week that would help me answer it better? A book, a person to ask, a page of text. The bell holds the time.
Know who you work for. Rabbi Elazar's teaching: learn well enough to answer the skeptic, and remember before whom you toil.
screen: `KNOW WHO YOU WORK FOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: know who you work for. Today, look up one real answer to a hard question you've been avoiding. Day two hundred sixty-two.

263.title: The day is short (Avot 2:15)
263.hook: Rabbi Tarfon: the day is short, the work is great, the workers are lazy
263.howItsDone: Rabbi Tarfon's saying is often quoted in Jewish teaching as a reminder that life is brief and there is much good to do, and it is usually paired with the saying that follows it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Elazar: know what to answer the skeptic, and know before whom you toil. Your line was know who you work for. What hard question did you look into? Day two hundred sixty-three.

It's four in the afternoon. You look at your list. Somehow the easy things got done: the emails, the small errands, a very thorough reorganization of your desk. And the one hard thing, the thing that actually mattered, is still sitting at the top of the list, untouched. The light is already changing. Rabbi Tarfon, a priest who lived through the years when the Temple was destroyed, knew that four o'clock feeling. And he wrote it down in five short phrases that sound like a foreman shouting across a building site.
screen: `FOUR IN THE AFTERNOON.` → `THE HARD THING, UNTOUCHED.` → `A FOREMAN ON A BUILDING SITE.`

segments.voice: Here's Rabbi Tarfon. The day is short. The work is great. The workers are lazy. The reward is great. And the master of the house is pressing. Picture the world he's describing. In ancient Israel, a day laborer worked from sunrise to sundown, and the Torah said he had to be paid before the sun went down. So the whole day has a clock on it. When the light's gone, it's gone. Now read the saying as a picture of a life. The day is short: a lifetime goes faster than anyone expects. The work is great: there's so much to learn, so much good to do, so many people who need something. The workers are lazy: that's us, honestly. Not wicked. Just distracted, tired, reorganizing the desk. The reward is great: the work is worth it, more than we can see. And the master of the house is pressing: God, in this picture, is the owner of the field, and there's a gentle urgency in the air. Notice what Rabbi Tarfon doesn't say. He doesn't say you're a failure, or it's hopeless. He just names the situation as plainly as a foreman would, and trusts you to do the math. If the day is short and the work is great, you start with the thing that matters most. And if this sounds like a lot of pressure, hold on. Tomorrow, the very next line of Pirkei Avot, from the same Rabbi Tarfon, lets you breathe again.
screen: `FIVE SHORT PHRASES.` · `PAID BEFORE SUNDOWN.` · `A LIFE IS A WORKING DAY.` · `START WITH WHAT MATTERS MOST.` · then, large: `THE DAY IS SHORT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Let today's list come to mind. Notice which item you keep circling around. The hard one. The one that matters. Don't feel guilty about it. Just see it clearly. Then picture the first five minutes of doing it, right after this. Where you'll sit. What you'll open. The first sentence, the first call, the first step. The bell holds the time.
The day is short. Rabbi Tarfon's five phrases: the day is short, the work is great, the workers are lazy, the reward is great, the master is pressing.
Your line: the day is short. Today, start the hard thing first, before the easy ones fill up the light. Day two hundred sixty-three.

264.title: Not yours to finish (Avot 2:16)
264.hook: Rabbi Tarfon: it is not yours to finish the work, nor are you free to give it up
264.howItsDone: Rabbi Tarfon's words are among the most quoted in Pirkei Avot, often cited by Jews working on long efforts for justice, learning and repair that no one person can complete.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Tarfon, the foreman: the day is short, the work is great. Your line was the day is short. Did you start the hard thing first? Today, he lets you breathe. Day two hundred sixty-four.

Some problems are too big for one life. Hunger. Loneliness. A broken family pattern that goes back generations. A neighborhood that needs a hundred things. You look at them and two feelings arrive together. One says, it's hopeless, why bother. The other says, it's all on me, and I'm failing. Both feelings are exhausting, and both make people quit. Yesterday Rabbi Tarfon told us the day is short and the work is great. Today, in the very next line, he answers both feelings at once, in a sentence that people have been writing on walls and in notebooks ever since.
screen: `TOO BIG FOR ONE LIFE.` → `HOPELESS, OR ALL ON ME.` → `THE VERY NEXT LINE.`

segments.voice: Here's what Rabbi Tarfon says. It is not upon you to finish the work. But you are not free to walk away from it. Two halves, and each one answers a different fear. To the one who says it's all on me: it isn't. You were never asked to finish. The work is bigger than one life, and it was always meant to be. You do your part, and hand it on. To the one who says it's hopeless: you're still not free to quit. The Hebrew phrase is ben chorin, a free person, the same words used for a slave who's been set free. You're not that kind of free, not from this. You still owe your piece. There's a beautiful story in the Talmud that fits right beside this. Honi, a famous sage, is walking along a road when he sees an old man planting a carob tree. How long until it gives fruit? Honi asks. Seventy years, says the man. Do you really think you'll live seventy more years? And the old man answers: I found carob trees in the world when I came into it. My ancestors planted them for me, and I'm planting for my children. That's the whole teaching in one scene. He won't finish. He won't eat the fruit. And he plants anyway. Rabbi Tarfon ends his saying by returning to the employer from two days ago: the one you work for is trustworthy, and will pay your wage. You don't have to see the harvest to know the planting counts.
screen: `NOT UPON YOU TO FINISH.` · `NOT FREE TO WALK AWAY.` · `BEN CHORIN: A FREE PERSON.` · `HONI AND THE CAROB TREE.` · then, large: `DON'T FINISH, DON'T QUIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your piece. Settle, and breathe. Think of one big problem that weighs on you, in your family, your town, the world. Let yourself feel how big it is. Then set down the part that was never yours: finishing it. Feel that weight go. Now look for your piece, the small, real part you could do. One call, one hour, one kindness, one seed. Hold that piece in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Not yours to finish. Rabbi Tarfon's balance: it's not upon you to finish the work, and you're not free to walk away from it.
Your line: don't finish, don't quit. Today, do your part of one big thing, and let the rest belong to the people after you. Day two hundred sixty-four.

what a scholar hears: ben chorin, the phrase for a freed slave, is the freedom the saying denies: you're never released from your piece.

265.title: Who is wise? (Avot 4:1)
265.hook: Ben Zoma: the wise learn from everyone; the rich are content with their lot
265.howItsDone: Ben Zoma's four questions are among the best-known lines of Pirkei Avot, often taught to children, and many Jews quote 'who is rich? one who is happy with his portion' as a guide to contentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Tarfon: the work is not yours to finish, and you're not free to quit. Your line was don't finish, don't quit. What was your piece? Today, we skip ahead to chapter four. Day two hundred sixty-five.

The Talmud tells a story about a sage named Ben Zoma. One day he stood on a high step on the Temple Mount and looked down at the enormous crowds of pilgrims. And instead of being annoyed by all the people, he said a blessing. Think how hard the first human had to work for a piece of bread, he said. Plowing, sowing, reaping, threshing, grinding, kneading, baking. And I wake up, and all of it's been done for me, by all these people. That's the man who opens chapter four of Pirkei Avot, with four questions.
screen: `BEN ZOMA ON THE TEMPLE MOUNT.` → `ALL THESE PEOPLE.` → `FOUR QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Ben Zoma asks: who is wise? Who is strong? Who is rich? Who is honored? Each answer flips what you'd expect. Today, two of them. Who is wise? Not the one with the most degrees. The one who learns from every person. Then he gives a verse from the Psalms. In its plain sense, the verse says something almost boastful. In the old King James wording: "I have more understanding than all my teachers." But the Mishnah reads the Hebrew another way, which the words can bear: from all my teachers I gained understanding. Every person, then, is a teacher. The toddler who asks why. The coworker you find difficult. The stranger who does a job you've never noticed. Everyone knows something you don't. Who is rich? Not the one with the most. The one who's happy with his portion. What he already has. Another psalm backs it up: when you eat the work of your own hands, you'll be happy, and it will be well with you. Now go back to the Temple Mount. Ben Zoma looked at a huge crowd and saw bakers, farmers, weavers, all the people whose work fed and clothed him. He learned from everyone, and he was grateful for what he had. Wise and rich, both at once. Tomorrow, the other two questions. Today, the lesson is that wisdom and wealth begin in the same place: paying attention to the people around you, and to what you've already been given.
screen: `FOUR QUESTIONS THAT FLIP.` · `WISE: LEARNS FROM EVERY PERSON.` · `A PSALM, READ ANOTHER WAY.` · `RICH: HAPPY WITH HIS PORTION.` · then, large: `LEARN FROM EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your unexpected teachers. Settle, and breathe. Think of three people you'll likely see today, including one you don't especially like. For each one, ask: what does this person know that I don't? A skill, a kind of patience, a way of seeing. Don't hurry. There's always something. Then, for a breath or two, just notice something you already have that's enough. The bell holds the time.
Who is wise? Ben Zoma's answer: the one who learns from every person. And who is rich? The one who's happy with what he has.
Your line: learn from everyone. Today, ask one unexpected person how they do something, and really listen to the answer. Day two hundred sixty-five.

266.title: Who is strong? (Avot 4:1)
266.hook: Ben Zoma: the strong master their impulses; the honored honor others
266.howItsDone: Jewish ethics describes the lifelong work of mastering the yetzer hara, the selfish inclination, and many Jews learn Ben Zoma's four questions as children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ben Zoma: the wise learn from every person, and the rich are happy with their portion. Your line was learn from everyone. Who taught you something unexpected? Day two hundred sixty-six.

Somebody cuts you off in traffic. Your hands tighten on the wheel. The horn is right there. So is a gesture, and a whole paragraph of words you'd never say in front of your grandmother. And then, sometimes, something else happens. You breathe out, and let it go, and the car ahead just becomes a car again. Nobody sees it. Nobody gives you a medal. But Ben Zoma would say you just did the strongest thing anyone did on that road all day.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `THE HORN IS RIGHT THERE.` → `YOU LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Ben Zoma's third question: who is strong? The Hebrew word is gibor, the word for a warrior, a hero. And his answer: the one who conquers his own inclination. The urge, the impulse, the thing that wants to explode or grab or get even. Then he brings a verse from Proverbs, which in the old King James wording says: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Imagine that. Conquering a city is a king's glory. Ruling your own temper is greater. The battlefield Ben Zoma cares about is inside you. And then the fourth question: who is honored? You'd think the one everyone bows to. Ben Zoma says: the one who honors others. The verse he brings is about God: those who honor Me, I will honor. The commentators notice that Ben Zoma applies it to people, and explain that honoring people made in God's image is a way of honoring God. And there's a practical truth in it too. Honor you demand is fragile. Honor you give away tends to come back. So Ben Zoma's four questions flip the world: the wise learn, the strong hold back, the rich are content, and the honored give honor. And that ends a week of sayings: for heaven's sake, not rote, know who you work for, the day is short, don't finish, don't quit, learn from everyone, and today, strong is self-mastered.
screen: `GIBOR: THE WARRIOR.` · `THE ONE WHO CONQUERS HIS URGE.` · `SLOW TO ANGER, BETTER THAN MIGHTY.` · `HONORED: THE ONE WHO HONORS.` · then, large: `STRONG IS SELF-MASTERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse the strong moment. Settle, and breathe. Think of a situation where your temper usually wins. A certain person, a certain tone of voice, a certain kind of mess in the kitchen. Picture it starting. Feel the heat rise. Now, in your imagination, pause. One slow breath out. Let the heat pass through you without doing anything. That pause is the strength. Practice it a few times. The bell holds the time.
Who is strong? Ben Zoma's answer: the one who conquers his own inclination. And who is honored? The one who honors others.
Your line: strong is self-mastered. Today, when your temper rises, take one slow breath before you act, and honor one person out loud. Day two hundred sixty-six.

fork.setup: someone cuts you off in traffic and your hand is on the horn. what would Ben Zoma call strong?
options: lean on the horn. they need to learn.
breathe out and let it go.
follow them and make a point.
fork.reveal: who is strong? the one who conquers his own inclination. slow to anger is better than the mighty.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: who is strong? gibor is the word for a warrior.

trapdoor: what you thought: strong means powerful.
what it means: the real strength is mastering your own impulses, and real honor comes from giving it.
what a scholar hears: the honor verse is about God honoring those who honor God; Ben Zoma applies it to honoring people.
